note: Sow into a moist, firm seedbed. Late sowing lowers yield potential, early sowing raises the risk of aphids and disease.
The seed needs moist soil to germinate; a dry seedbed delays it and gives an uneven crop.
Shoots break the soil surface; uniform emergence sets up an even canopy for optimal light interception.
Plants develop side shoots to build ear number capacity; manage nitrogen early to support tiller survival.
Rapid stem elongation begins, demanding high water and nutrient uptake; protect against lodging and early fungal diseases.
The flag leaf expands and the ear swells within the sheath; keeping the flag leaf healthy is critical for grain filling.
Ears emerge from the sheath; flowering timing dictates potential grain count, requiring protection from Fusarium head blight.
Flowering is extremely sensitive to drought and heat; stress here causes severe sterile florets and slashes final yield.
Grains contain milky fluid; steady soil moisture is vital to prevent shrivelled kernels and secure grain weight.
Grains solidify into a starchy dough; dry down begins, and final kernel dry mass is largely locked in.
Grain moisture drops to harvest levels, signalling that the crop is ready to be combined before wet weather ruins quality.
